In [[mathematics]], a [[differential field]] ''K'' is '''differentially closed''' if every finite system of [[differential equation]]s with a solution in some differential field extending ''K'' already has a solution in ''K''. This concept was introduced by {{harvtxt|Robinson|1959}}. Differentially closed fields are the analogues
for differential equations of [[algebraically closed field]]s for polynomial equations.

== The theory of differentially closed fields==

We recall that a [[differential field]] is a [[Field (mathematics)|field]] equipped with a [[Derivation (abstract algebra)|derivation]] operator. Let ''K'' be a differential field with derivation operator ∂.

*A '''differential polynomial''' in ''x'' is a polynomial in the formal expressions ''x'', ∂''x'', ∂<sup>2</sup>''x'', ... with coefficients in ''K''.
*The '''order''' of a non-zero differential polynomial in ''x'' is the largest ''n'' such that ∂<sup>''n''</sup>''x'' occurs in it, or &minus;1 if the differential polynomial is a constant.
*The '''separant''' ''S''<sub>''f''</sub> of a differential polynomial of order ''n''≥0 is the derivative of ''f'' with respect to ∂<sup>''n''</sup>''x''.
*The '''field of constants''' of ''K'' is the subfield of elements ''a'' with ∂''a''=0.
*In a differential field ''K'' of nonzero [[Characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] ''p'', all ''p''th powers are constants. It follows that neither ''K'' nor its field of constants is [[Perfect field|perfect]], unless ∂ is trivial. A field ''K'' with derivation ∂ is called '''differentially perfect''' if it is either of characteristic 0, or of characteristic ''p'' and every constant is a ''p''th power of an element of ''K''.
*A '''differentially closed field''' is a differentially perfect differential field ''K''  such that if ''f'' and ''g'' are  differential polynomials such that  ''S''<sub>''f''</sub>≠ 0 and ''g''≠0 and  ''f'' has order greater than that of ''g'', then there is some ''x'' in ''K'' with ''f''(''x'')=0 and ''g''(''x'')≠0. (Some authors add the condition that  ''K'' has characteristic 0, in which case ''S''<sub>''f''</sub> is automatically non-zero, and ''K'' is automatically perfect.)
*'''DCF<sub>''p''</sub>''' is the theory of differentially closed fields of characteristic ''p'' (where ''p'' is 0 or a prime).

Taking ''g''=1 and ''f'' any ordinary [[separable polynomial]] shows that any differentially closed field is [[separably closed]]. In characteristic 0 this implies that it is algebraically closed, but in characteristic ''p''>0 differentially closed fields are never algebraically closed.

Unlike the complex numbers in the theory of algebraically closed fields, there is no  natural example of a differentially closed field.
Any differentially perfect field ''K'' has a '''differential closure''', a  [[prime model]] extension, which is differentially closed. Shelah showed that the differential closure is unique up to isomorphism over ''K''. Shelah also showed that the prime differentially closed field of characteristic 0 (the differential closure of the rationals) is not [[minimal model (set theory)|minimal]]; this was a rather surprising result, as it is not what one would expect by analogy with algebraically closed fields.

The theory of  DCF<sub>''p''</sub> is [[complete theory|complete]] and [[model complete]] (for ''p''=0 this was shown by Robinson, and for ''p''>0 by {{harvtxt|Wood|1973}}).
The theory DCF<sub>''p''</sub> is the [[model companion]] of the theory of differential fields of characteristic ''p''. It is  the model completion of the theory of differentially perfect fields of characteristic ''p'' if one adds to the language a symbol giving the ''p''th root of constants when ''p''>0. The theory of differential fields of characteristic ''p''>0 does not have a model completion, and in characteristic ''p''=0 is the same as the theory of differentially perfect fields so has DCF<sub>0</sub> as its model completion.

The number of differentially closed fields of some infinite [[cardinality]] κ is 2<sup>κ</sup>; for κ uncountable this was proved by {{harvtxt|Shelah|1973}}, and for κ countable by Hrushovski and Sokolovic.

== The Kolchin topology ==

The ''Kolchin topology'' on ''K'' <sup>m</sup> is defined by taking sets of solutions of systems of differential equations over ''K'' in ''m'' variables as basic closed sets.  Like the [[Zariski topology]], the Kolchin topology is [[Noetherian topological space|Noetherian]].

A d-constructible set is a finite union of closed and open sets in the Kolchin topology. Equivalently, a d-constructible set is the set of solutions to a quantifier-free, or [[atomic formula|atomic]], formula with parameters in ''K''.

== Quantifier elimination ==

Like the theory of algebraically closed fields, the theory DCF<sub>0</sub> of differentially closed fields of characteristic 0 [[quantifier elimination|eliminates quantifiers]].  The geometric content of this statement is that the projection of a d-constructible set is d-constructible. It also eliminates imaginaries, is complete, and model complete.

In characteristic ''p''>0, the theory DCF<sub>p</sub> eliminates quantifiers in the language of differential fields with a unary function ''r'' added that is the ''p''th root of all constants, and is 0 on elements that are not constant.

== Differential Nullstellensatz ==
The differential Nullstellensatz is the analogue in differential algebra of Hilbert's [[nullstellensatz]].

*A '''differential ideal''' or ∂-ideal is an ideal closed under ∂.
*An ideal is called '''radical''' if it contains all roots of its elements.

Suppose that ''K'' is a differentially closed field of characteristic 0. <!-- I'm not sure whether characteristic 0 is necessary-->. Then Seidenberg's '''differential nullstellensatz''' states  there is a [[bijection]] between
*Radical differential ideals in the ring of differential polynomials in ''n'' variables, and
*∂-closed subsets of ''K''<sup>''n''</sup>.
This correspondence maps a ∂-closed subset to the ideal of elements vanishing on it, and maps an ideal to its set of zeros.

== Omega stability ==
In characteristic 0 Blum showed that the theory of differentially closed fields is [[ω-stable]] and  has [[Morley rank]] ω.{{CN|date=January 2023}}
In non-zero characteristic {{harvtxt|Wood|1973}} showed that the theory of differentially closed fields is not ω-stable, and {{harvtxt|Shelah|1973}} showed more precisely that it is [[stable theory|stable]] but not [[superstable]].
